segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I watched as the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and there was a white horse, and its rider had a bow. A crown was given to him, and he went out conquering and to conquer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And out came another horse, fiery red. It was given to its rider to take peace from the earth, so that people would slaughter one another, and a great sword was given to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and there was a black horse, and its rider had a pair of scales in his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius—and do not harm the oil and the wine!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and there was a pale green horse. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed along with him. They were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with plague, and by the wild animals of the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slaughtered because of the word of God and because of the testimony they held.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They cried out with a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How long, Master, holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who live on the earth?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the number was made complete of their fellow slaves and brothers and sisters who were about to be killed as they themselves had been.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I watched when he opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake; the sun became black as sackcloth made of hair, and the whole moon became like blood,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the stars of the sky fell to the earth, as a fig tree drops its unripe figs when shaken by a strong wind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sky was split apart like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the kings of the earth and the nobles and the commanders and the rich and the powerful, and every slave and free person, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they said to the mountains and the rocks,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for the great day of their wrath has come, and who is able to stand?”

notes.note: Many manuscripts add “and see” here and at the other three summonses, which makes the command an invitation to John; the King James Version follows that reading. Without the addition, the command is most naturally a summons to the horseman who then appears. The Greek verb can also mean “Go!”, and some translators render it that way.

The identity of the first rider is disputed. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, take him to be Christ or the advance of the gospel, pointing to the white horse of chapter 19. Most scholars today see him as military conquest, the first of four parallel disasters, with the bow suggesting a mounted archer. The crown is the victor’s wreath, and “conquer” is the same verb used in the promises to “the one who conquers” in the letters to the seven churches.

notes.phrase: A quart of wheat for a denarius
notes.traditional: A measure of wheat for a penny
notes.note: The Greek measure, the choinix, held roughly a liter of grain, about one person’s daily ration, and a denarius was about a day’s wage for a laborer. These are famine prices, several times the normal rate: a day’s work buys only enough wheat for one person, or enough of the cheaper barley for a small household. Why the oil and wine are to be spared is debated; it may limit the famine’s severity or point to the bitter irony of luxuries surviving while bread fails.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for the green of plants (it is used of grass elsewhere in Revelation) and was also used for the yellowish-green pallor of the sick or dying. “Pale” alone loses the color; “pale green” keeps both the hue and the suggestion of a corpse. Several modern versions do the same.

The Greek word is the same as the rider’s name, “Death.” In the Greek Old Testament this word regularly translates the Hebrew term for pestilence, and the list here echoes Ezekiel 14:21, where God’s four judgments are sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. Most modern translations therefore have “plague” or “pestilence”; the King James Version keeps “death.”

In Israel’s sacrificial worship the blood of a victim, which was understood to carry its life, was poured out at the base of the altar. The picture presents those killed for their testimony as sacrifices, slaughtered like the Lamb himself; the same verb is used of both. Whether the altar of burnt offering or the incense altar is in view is debated.

This is not the usual New Testament word for “Lord” but the term for the master of a household and owner of slaves, also used in prayer to God as absolute ruler. Many modern versions render it “Sovereign Lord”; the King James Version has “O Lord.” “Master” keeps it distinct from the ordinary word and preserves the link with “fellow slaves” in the next verse.

The Greek word means someone who shares the condition of a slave under the same master. Most English versions soften it to “fellow servants.” Here it answers the address to God as “Master” in the previous verse. The “fellow slaves” and the “brothers and sisters” are probably one group described in two ways, though the Greek could also be read as two groups.

notes.phrase: until the number was made complete
notes.note: The Greek says literally “until their fellow slaves … were completed.” Most translators take this to mean that a set number of martyrs must be reached, an idea found in other Jewish writings of the period. Some manuscripts have an active form, “until they complete,” which would mean until the others finish their course.

notes.phrase: the sun became black as sackcloth made of hair
notes.traditional: the sun became black as sackcloth of hair
notes.note: The signs in verses 12–14 draw on the prophets’ pictures of the day of the Lord: the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood in Joel 2:31, and the heavens rolled up like a scroll with their host falling like fruit from a fig tree in Isaiah 34:4. The cry to the mountains in verse 16 echoes Hosea 10:8. Sackcloth was coarse dark cloth, usually of goat hair, worn in mourning.

The Greek word covers both the visible sky and God’s dwelling. Here and in verse 14 the stars and the visible vault overhead are meant, so “sky” is used, as in a number of modern versions; older versions have “heaven.”

The verb means to separate or part. The picture may be of the sky splitting and curling back on itself like a scroll, or of the sky being removed altogether, as when a scroll is rolled up and put away; hence renderings such as “vanished” or “receded.” The Greek does not settle which is meant.

The manuscripts are divided between “their wrath,” referring to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, and “his wrath.” The King James Version follows the latter; most modern editions and translations read “their,” judging that scribes were more likely to change the plural to match the preceding “wrath of the Lamb” than the reverse.

candidates.reason: The choice between “slave” and “servant” (and the matching “fellow slave” for σύνδουλος in verse 11) recurs across the whole New Testament and should not vary by chapter.
The plural used of community members is rendered “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” or “believers” by different versions, and readers would be misled if it varied between chapters.
Used of God and Christ in Luke, Acts, 2 Peter, Jude and Revelation, and of slave owners in the Pastorals and 1 Peter; versions split between “Sovereign Lord,” “Master” and “Lord.”
The throne-room beings of Revelation are “beasts” in the KJV and “living creatures” in modern versions, and must stay distinct from θηρίον, “beast” or “wild animal,” throughout the book.
Versions alternate between “authority,” “power” and “right” across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, and the distinction from δύναμις is easily blurred without a fixed decision.
